We demonstrate a particular ordering of sets of zeros of Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ that can be derived from the corresponding sets of zeros of Eisenstein series for $GL(n-1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, and vice versa. Furthermore, we establish a combinatorial approach to understanding how zeros of Eisenstein series on $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ are generated from the zeros of Eisenstein series on $GL(n-1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

This study develops a novel biophysical model of brain dysfunction associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing a computational framework that integrates advanced imaging techniques and pharmacological data from marmoset monkeys. By combining hyperspectral functional magnetic resonance imaging and electrical current stimulation, the model identifies abnormal circuit patterns characteristic of Parkinson's disease in the marmoset brain. To achieve this, a multi-region circuit model was implemented, incorporating 57 brain areas connected by 157 regions in the marmoset monkey central nervous system. Utilizing a computational framework that considers multiple brain regions as interconnected electrical circuits, the model includes highly specialized computer code that simulates the unique electrical properties of brain cells, synaptic connections, and the flow of electrical currents through the brain. With proper permission from the original authors, the model was modified and a numerical solution was developed using advanced computational techniques. By adjusting key components of the model, including the strength of cellular electrical properties and synaptic connections, the development of computational protocols was initiated to match the model to experimental data from monkeys treated with the drug rotigotine. Through this protocol, the model was successfully matched to show the same levels of brain circuit function observed when rotigotine is administered to Parkinson's disease patients. With the permission of the original authors, the model was further modified to mimic the effects of rotigotine and the progression of Parkinson's disease. Through this modification, the development of computational protocols was initiated to match the model to experimental data from monkeys that do not receive rotig

Achieving a perfect balance between visual quality and performance in map visualization can be challenging, especially when rendering large numbers of lines to accommodate global positioning system (GPS) coordinates, where even minor improvements can have a significant impact. To further complicate matters, many modern mapping applications involve connecting lines to specific locations on a map, which can lead to visualization artifacts and distortion. In our research, we focus on enhancing the appearance of line connections by applying a novel anti-aliasing technique, one that maintains performance by leveraging graphics hardware capabilities. Our approach, which incorporates a telescoping pattern to mimic the desired shape while reducing rendering instructions, offers a suitable alternative to existing methods like font-based rendering and conservative rasterization. Our results show that our technique yields a notable enhancement in visual quality with only a minimal performance cost, making it an ideal solution for high-quality map visualization.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and belonging to the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes.

We develop a novel set of interpolation functions that maintain a consistent form for both exact and approximate interpolation purposes. This formulation is particularly useful for creating smooth surfaces from scattered data, with a unique characteristic being that it naturally produces a conservative interpolation form. Unlike traditional methods that employ piecewise interpolation, our approach maintains a continuous and consistent form globally. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we compare it with the method of Chen and Wu, using data presented in their journal article.

Understanding the Earth's climate is crucial, and central to this understanding are extensive observations made through satellite imagery of different types. Unfortunately, annotating these images with accuracy and speed is a challenge due to the complexity of climate data and the need for highly specialized expertise. As a result, using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) becomes attractive for both segmenting and classifying climate types directly from satellite images. However, there are several issues with existing datasets, including limited class distinctions and small image samples, which significantly impede CNNs' generalization ability. To address these problems, we created the ClimateCategorization dataset with five distinct climate classes and a vast range of annotated images, along with a novel multi-channel data enhancement approach that utilizes local contrast information to inform global adjustments. Nevertheless, our research reveals that, despite the advances in CNNs, they still struggle to effectively generalize across different data formats, annotation stability, and parallel processing, which is further compromised by the use of outdated datasets. As such, we propose a sequential training strategy that combines a super-resolution technique to improve climate classification and a global modification of our enhancement approach to accommodate annotation variations. Although the results we obtained are promising, they highlight the importance of creating more comprehensive and up-to-date datasets to facilitate the development of more generalizable climate classification models.

To develop more efficient and flexible speech enhancement algorithms, separate processing of individual frequency bins has been proposed. Building on this idea, a Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model has been presented that proceeds in two approaches. The first approach involves a single, integrated system of recurrent and convolutional networks. This system is then replicated independently for each frequency bin in the second approach. Research has demonstrated that the dual-path configuration leads to better performance, with an 0.31 dB average improvement in NSR over the single-path model. Furthermore, the DPCRN model exhibits compelling training and evaluation efficiency, needing only 5 seconds per epoch on a single GPU.

The addition of neutrino mass within a specific class of $f(R)$ gravity models could potentially alter the typical behavior of dark matter, as observed in galaxy rotations and the cosmic large-scale structure. By examining three parameters - the neutrino mass, $f_R''(R=0)$, and $\Lambda$ - in a mathematical framework that represents these $f(R)$ gravity models, we explore their effects on the formation of dark matter structures through numerical simulations. Our results indicate that increasing the parameter $f_R''(R=0)$ while maintaining zero neutrino mass leads to a reduction in the turnover radius $r_{m*}$ by approximately $2.5$ kpc, which could be as high as $5$ kpc when neutrino mass is included. Furthermore, our analysis reveals distinct differences between traditional $\Lambda$CDM and these $f(R)$ gravity models with neutrino mass at $r_{m*}$, resulting from changes in density profile. However, we find that density profile changes are less pronounced with modified initial conditions, leading to a greater impact of neutrino mass over $f_R''(R=0)$. These findings have implications for searching for heavy neutrinos through galaxy structure, potentially offering a more sensitive test of certain $f(R)$ gravity models.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric circulation by distinguishing between separate temperature bands within the atmosphere. This study takes an initial step towards evaluating these models using a simple atmospheric circulation model based on Rayleigh-Benard convection. The model is modified to accommodate a two-fluid representation, where distinct temperature layers undergo convection independently while interacting through surface heat transfer. A comprehensive assessment of the model's performance is conducted under various convection regimes ranging from lightly disturbed to highly turbulent conditions. The analysis reveals that the model's simulation results struggle to accurately capture certain aspects of convection dynamics despite showing some similarity to the actual convection patterns. Further examination of the results highlights several key issues, including the appearance of spurious velocity oscillations, discrepancies in momentum transfer simulations, and failures in correctly modeling fluid development near the edges of the heated plate. Several potential solutions are also explored to address these limitations, including the implementation of different collision counter measures and increased viscosity levels. Ultimately, the study finds that the model's simulation results become more accurate when using a more sophisticated convection algorithm. The evaluation of the model's performance is detailed in a comprehensive set of figures and diagrams.

We investigate a scenario where two independent Jaynes-Cummings systems, representing two atomic sources, undergo an quantum interaction. Our analysis focuses on identifying the conditions under which the joint system exhibits an entangled state, given that the individual atomic sources are initially uncorrelated. Using applications in quantum metrology and entanglement switcing as context, we show that the entangled state of the joint system can lead to an precision improvement by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$ over the non-entangled state, where $N$ is the number of independent JC interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entangled state can be achieved with realistic experimental set-ups using JC systems based on superconducting devices or semiconducting quantum dots.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an updated forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and improved material composition was tested in conjunction with the existing CMS setup. This protocol prototype demonstrated capability in identifying particle events, and thus this paper presents the technical details and technical performance of the updated forward pixel detector, specifically the pixel prototype's reconstruction component. Specifically, it highlights the protocol's construction, the reconstruction algorithm used, and the prototype's overall performance following several thousand hours of operation.

A method using Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation is effective in determining the spectrum of the SU(2) glueball for a lattice QCD simulation. This approach is pertinent as it bypasses the use of operators with specific quantum numbers, allowing for an direct inspection of the glueball spectrum from the correlation function alone. Our analysis of the 0$^{-+}$ channel reveals a clear spectral signal at a mass eigenvalue of approximately 1.642(18) for a specific range of momenta, in line with prior studies. Moreover, we've established the spectral representation for the 0$^{++}$ SU(2) glueball mass across a range of momenta, and it demonstrates the expected behavior of a ground state.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
Due to the rapid posting of tweets, it's essential to use an automatic approach to classify
emotions as supervised learning methods are used here, but maintaining accuracy over time
is challenging due to the constantly shifting nature of language used on Twitter. Many
machine learning models have been proposed for sentiment analysis on Twitter, but few can
handle the issues mentioned above. This paper proposes a sentiment analysis model using
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with word and character-level word embeddings to achieve
better results. The model leverages the basic LSTM model by incorporating a memory cell
and a coordinator module to classify emotions, and it's trained on the Sentiment140 dataset
with a focus on selecting the optimal embedding size. The model's performance is then evaluated
on the same dataset, and the results show that the proposed model performs well even when
general-purpose embedding is used. The model's performance is also evaluated on a dataset
with a longer text length, and the findings suggest that the proposed model outperforms
other machine learning models, including a basic LSTM model. The model's performance can
be improved by replacing the memory cell with a recurrent module, and the findings may
not be generalize to other datasets due to the limited size of the dataset used

A nonlinear interaction exists between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

The tomographic representation of quantum states offers a comprehensive view of a quantum system's properties and dynamics. This form of representation is particularly useful for studying the entanglement and synchronization of continuous-variable systems. We examine the tomographic patterns of Wigner functions in these systems to identify their entanglement and characterize the synchronization phenomenon. Specifically, we analyze the effects of increasing the number of oscillators in a linear chain and the strength of the coupling between them. Our findings reveal that as the number of oscillators increases, the tomographic patterns transition from an unstable, chaotic form to a stable, periodic form, marking a shift from system decoupling to synchronization. Systems exhibiting entanglement show distinct, rotating tomographic patterns, whereas unentangled systems display stationary patterns. Additionally, we find that in entangled systems, increasing the number of oscillators leads to a decrease in entanglement, while strengthening the coupling between oscillators increases entanglement.

Conversational interfaces have seen significant advancements in recent times, offering engaging experiences to users through natural language interactions. By leveraging AI technology, characters in media like film and video games have become more immersive with developed personalities and behaviors. Building upon this progress, we have developed a role-defined conversation framework using large-scale language models, enabling it to exhibit a defined personality while maintaining the ability to engage in spontaneous conversations about various topics. This framework combines multiple LLMs to create multiple personality profiles, allowing it to participate in conversations on its own or with the input of a human user. We then tested this framework's capability by evaluating the personalities it was programmed with and collecting a dataset of conversations it had with other users. We found that it successfully incorporated human-like language elements and was enjoyable to interact with, even after many conversations. Furthermore, we observed that the conversations it had with other users were similar to normal human conversations when analyzed at a larger scale. We are now exploring ways to provide more context to the conversation model and incorporating additional features like a memory element to enhance the personalities it was programmed with and the human-like language elements it uses.

Optimal control techniques are utilized to model the population dynamics of pests and other regulatory species in controlled environments. The Strong Technique framework leverages an exact solution to the optimal control problem to create a suitable approximation. This approximation does not require the formulation of an Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation and instead employs a direct approach. As a result, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation does not contain switching surfaces, which are typically difficult to determine. The advantages of this method are demonstrated through an application to the management of disease in strawberry crops, where the population growth of two species, namely strawberry pests and their natural predators, are modeled. By allocating a limited amount of control to each species, the model aims to minimize population levels and reduce the spread of a damaging disease. The Strong Technique framework is used to solve this problem in a controlled environment.

360-degree virtual travel videos offer engaging and immersive experiences, but presenting this information through subtitles can facilitate a different viewing perspective. This new paradigm is called subtitle-driven viewing, which enables users to focus on information while ignoring the visual content. However, the ability to anticipate upcoming information, known as forecast, is missing from current 360-degree video systems. To address this, we present a novel approach called VPF (Viewport Prediction Framework), which utilizes data on subtitles and audio to forecast the upcoming region of interest. Through user studies and evaluation, our method demonstrates its superiority over control conditions and showcases the significance of VPF in enhancing the viewing experience of 360-degree virtual travel videos.

Tensor network methods have successfully modeled diverse quantum states,  but their application to dynamic situations is limited due to their reversible and causal neutrality.  This research adapts the finite-temperature algebraic decomposition method (fATMDMGPT) to describe both thermal states and time-evolution in quantum systems,  allowing for a precise, local interpretation of the tensor network architecture.  A novel factorization for the time-evolution operator is introduced with a structured path order that mimics the direction of time,  while users can specify the initial thermal condition using a coherent state factorization.  This approach is demonstrated through simulations of a Dimer model and a bulk transport phenomenon in a 1D Wire system.  The proposed fATMDMGPT framework provides a versatile tool for studying quantum dynamics out of equilibrium.

We develop a decoupling theory for a class of heavy-tailed claims with depending dimensions, building on a novel finding that assumes approximately independent components. A statistical test is designed to verify the accuracy of certain assumptions made throughout our analysis. Our method for evaluating risk is based on a new approach that accounts for relying dimensions and uses a testable condition to ensure consistency. As a result, our approach provides a more efficient estimation method than traditional techniques.

In this research, we establish a nonisotropic $p$-capacity inequality that mirrors the principles of the classic Beyke-Kinnunen-M\"{a}ki-Kurki-Nara theory, albeit within the context of nonhomogeneous isotropic spaces. Building upon this foundation, we then derive a nonisotropic Minkowski inequality as a direct consequence.

The Microscope space experiment, which operated between 2016 and 2017, was designed to test the equivalence principle at its most fundamental level. Based on measurements obtained using laser interferometry, the experiment estimated that the principle's violation does not exceed 10^-15. However, this achievement came with an significant statistical uncertainty, and there are concerns that certain sudden events, or glitches, could influence the results. Considering the extreme precision of this test, the study examines the statistical significance of these events and investigates their impact on the principle's validation. By accounting for the number and location of glitch occurrences within the measurement period, the study determines that none of these events significantly affect the principle's validity. Additionally, the study offers insights into the factors that contribute to these events and explores possible strategies for reducing their impact on future equivalence principle tests.

The movement of particles in complex environments is influenced by external forces and is further modified by forces arising from interactions with surrounding particles. These interactions create spatial variations in mechanical stress and the rotation of particles as they move. A new mathematical model describes how particles behave dynamically in environments that change activity levels spatially. By assuming that particle rotation rates are constant and can be set to zero, the model predicts various dynamics of particle motion, including steady-state motion, damped motion, and motion influenced by external forces. It also reveals how particles move in regions with varying activity levels, especially where activity decreases gradually and to a greater extent near a surface. The model shows that particles can also get trapped in areas with low activity levels due to external forces and a phenomenon known as shear banding.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for specific graphs and networks.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified in terms of the small-$x$ impact, aided by the Borel transformation, which transforms the expansion into a convergent integral form, and estimates from Borel summation, aided by the convolution term's asymptotic estimate and the small-$x$ filter, which indicates that the variance's impact is significant, in the range of 0.5 to 1.5, with the correct coefficient to influence Higgs boson production in proton-proton collisions via the vector boson fusion process, whereas the impact of infrared renormalons on the color dipole gluon distribution's mean is found to be much smaller, in the range of -0.01 to -0.001, which suggests that the variance's impact could be detected in experimental data with a precision of $10^{-3}$, or in experiments with an increased luminosity at a more precise level, and that the detection of the variance's impact would imply the identification of the infrared renormalon's role in the $x$-space, and potentially the Borel summation, in quantum chromodynamics, and that this detection could also have a significant impact on theoretical models, and that the impact of infrared renormalons on the color dipole gluon distribution's variance could be detected in other processes, such as jet production, and that the detection of this impact would imply the identification of

This study examines the amphibian model, which represents an election process, on a binary tree with three leaves labeled red, green, and blue. The model disperses chameleons between the leaves until they all agree on a color. The number of chameleons required to guarantee an majority outcome (red or blue) was previously established as (d+1)/2, where d represents the number of chameleons starting from an arbitrary color. However, the lower bound for this scenario was unknown. This research determines the minimal d for which an majority outcome is achievable and finds it to be equal to the largest number of leaves that can be separated by a hedgehog (representing (d+1)/2 chameleons) and provides evidence that the Cai-Ding lower bound estimate is overly conservative.

Researchers are focusing on ultrafast laser-written photonic surfaces to create dynamic microstructures for manipulating light. These surfaces can shape light based on the local index modification, but only respond to changes in the electric field. A new approach uses heat-sensitive magnetophotonic surfaces that respond to light intensity, enabling control over light through intensity rather than field. This concept is being explored through a novel surface lattice designed using sub-100 nm magnetophotonic filaments in the form of a microstructured glass surface. This structure exhibits increased magnetostatic pressure and a reduced local field, which, when excited by microjoule pulses, leads to enhanced temperature changes. As a result, this surface can switch its photon mode from linear to circular polarization in response to increased light intensity, demonstrating the potential of these structures for controlling light based on intensity. Next, a new approach involving van der Waals materials is proposed to expand the functioning of such surfaces to the visible range. Furthermore, an implementation of this structure in a form of magnetophotonic fiber is also proposed, which could enable the control of light based on intensity in fiber-based applications.

Deep neural networks achieve exceptional results in classifying medical images, yet their distribution is typically limited in training data and rich in real-world applications. The issue lies in their lack of inherent understanding of medical concepts, forcing them to rely on visual features learned during training. This research demonstrates that by simply relying on visual features, these networks can successfully classify medical conditions beyond their trained scope, a phenomenon referred to as Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL). To achieve this, a new decision-based black-box framework is introduced, utilizing a separate neural network to extract medical insights from the original network's predictions. This framework enables the extraction of medical expertise from publicly available datasets, allowing the original network to benefit from this knowledge in a zero-shot manner. Successful applications of this research include examples from breast biopsy image analysis and colon lesion classification, where a pre-trained network achieves comparable results to models trained with expanded datasets.

Investigating the decay sequences $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)} K^0_S$, this paper reports the first results of searches at the LHCb experiment for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays, where the $\bar{D}^{(*0)}$ system is reconstructed through the decay modes $\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $K^+ K^-$ respectively. Based on a data volume of 1.0 fnbart $B^0_s$ decays, the upper limit for the branching fraction of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ is found to be 3.5 $\times 10^{-4}$ at 95% confidence level, and there is a signal excess at 3.4 standard deviations above the background forecast for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays, with an estimated upper limit of 5.8 $\times 10^{-4}$ at 95% confidence level.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite some established methods for specific types of modules, such as cyclic and semisimple modules, the process remains largely unexplored for other modules. In this study, we focus on modules with a specific property – having no modules of certain complexity as submodules. We propose a method to construct the lattice of submodules of these modules using their composition series and the lattice of submodules of associated prime modules. We demonstrate this method by constructing the lattice of submodules of modules with this property – modules with non-zero simple submodules and modules with non-zero simple quotients. Additionally, we apply this method to modules with this property – modules with multiple composition series and modules with multiple associated prime modules.

This research investigates complex systems identified through a single geodetic measurement, considering the impact of simultaneous disturbances on systems with multiple inputs and outputs. The study's primary focus lies in determining the precision required for distinct component connections and developing efficient computational methods for allocating resources among a team of identifying engineers. The proposed approaches minimize the amount of data required for each engineer while ensuring the precise accuracy for identifying the system's components.

The objective of imitation learning is to train a model to behave like an expert based on a set of instructions, which are essentially examples of how the model should act in various situations. The key challenge in imitation learning is addressing a gap between the instructions and the model's current behavior. This issue is exacerbated when the instructions are limited, as the model lacks a comprehensive understanding of its possible outcomes and how to achieve the desired results. This problem is even more pronounced in complex tasks that require multiple actions to be completed, as the model must navigate the interplay between all actions at once. To overcome this difficulty, a new approach called TRAIL has been developed, which directly focuses on closing the gap between the instructions and the model's current behavior. This approach ensures that the model's behavior becomes increasingly similar to the desired outcome after each iteration of training. The result is a TRAIL-based algorithm that can learn from inadequate data, as it makes use of all available information to minimize the gap. In experiments, this algorithm performed better than existing methods, particularly in games and simulation tasks that require multiple actions. Additionally, it was more efficient and effective when there were many possible actions.

In complex systems, both observation and action skills are crucial for successful task execution. However, current robotic learning methods typically focus on individual observations and actions separately, neglecting the interplay between both. This paper introduces the concept of Co-Observation Learning, which involves training robots to enhance the observation capabilities of their fellow robots in a collaborative setting. We establish a framework for Co-Observation Learning without access to task demonstration data, leveraging observation-based feedback to guide learning. A complementary learning approach is proposed to address potential difficulties with mutual observation enhancement. This strategy involves learning a natural language instruction sequence for one robot to follow the instructions of another. Successful implementation of this approach is demonstrated through simulation experiments and in real-world tests, highlighting the benefits of Co-Observation Learning in areas like collaborative navigation and tool use.

This paper investigates the measurement of polarization in quantum systems using additive codes named PAC codes, specifically for an erasure channel. We propose a new method to determine the polarization of these codes and demonstrate that this method is effective in identifying the polarization of codes obtained from partial transmission. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the polarized code rates of a source encoder and the characteristics of the erasure channel. We show that the polarized code rates are dependent on the specific probabilities of erasure and are therefore unique to each channel. Furthermore, we provide a practical approach for computing the polarized code rates based on the characteristics of the source and the physical properties of the communication channel.

Using reinforcement learning to improve neural machine translation is a promising approach, but one significant challenge remains: many potential translation options exist, making the search process unfeasible. This difficulty is compounded by the large action spaces inherent in sequence generation tasks. In response, researchers have proposed various strategies to narrow down the action space, but their effectiveness has not been consistently evaluated across all translation scenarios. This paper investigates the use of a more extensive action space in reinforcement learning for neural machine translation, demonstrating that a targeted space with limited actions yields superior results compared to other strategies. Interestingly, our findings reveal that certain targeted action spaces lead to decreased performance, suggesting that the selection of action functions is critical. To produce the highest translation quality, we introduce the targeted action space reinforcement learning (TAS-RL) framework, which automatically identifies an optimal targeted action space through additional learning objectives. Our experimental results show that TAS-RL outperforms conventional reinforcement learning strategies on multiple targeted action spaces.

To facilitate effortless setup and precise calculations for robotic tasks in relation to a mounted camera, we develop a method using machine learning to automatically determine the robotic depth camera configuration and effector position. By utilizing a large dataset of configurations along with related radiation patterns, we create a novel approach involving minimum variance multilinear regression. This approach is straightforward to implement and efficient in terms of computational resources. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we utilize it in a setup featuring a robotic arm and a 2D camera. By establishing a direct correlation between radiation patterns and the geometric properties of these setups, we develop the MVLR model. We then optimize this model in a way that requires minimal assumptions, thereby eliminating the need for advanced camera calculations. By utilizing synthetic data along with radiation patterns generated through simulation, we showcase the capability of the MVLR model to accurately predict configuration specifics and camera positioning. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the model to real-world data, thereby proving that machine learning techniques can enhance the setup of robotic systems in relation to attached cameras.

Quantum quasifree fermion surfaces exhibit a unique 'fermion surface character' that is not observable in regular fermion surfaces. The name 'quantum quasifree fermion surface' captures the essence of this property, making regular fermion surfaces'standard' by comparison. The theory of quantum quasifree fermion surfaces was initially described in 1962 by Bogoliubov, Rostovtsev, and Shirkov, and it represents a key component of the Bogoliubov theory. This paper delves into the specifics of quantum quasifree fermion surfaces, including their energy spectrum, fermion number operator, and characteristic constants of motion. Additionally, it explores the relationship between quasifree fermion surfaces and Bogoliubov transformations.

The internet has significantly altered the way news is consumed, with individuals browsing news on various websites and social media platforms. Despite noticeable changes in overall behavior, thorough analysis of strategic action in this environment has been lagging behind. Our research focuses on revealing underlying mechanisms governing the spread of news on social media and the factors influencing individual behavior in this process. We implemented a new mechanism analysis on a dataset containing information about users who share news on Twitter, taking into account both personal characteristics and preferences as well as the effects of social influence. Our results show that individuals behave in a way that maximizes attention from others, prioritize users with similar political views, particularly those who are more active on Twitter, and are more likely to share news if they have a strong opinion on the issue mentioned in the news. Furthermore, we discovered that users can be categorized into two groups based on their behavior, one with a high degree of connectivity and another with a lower degree of connectivity. We found statistically significant differences in mail-in news consumption, higher degrees of connectivity in email news consumption, and higher costs for producing email news. Additionally, we found that users with a high degree of connectivity tend to place a higher value on entertainment, enjoy reading newspapers more, and are more active on Twitter, have a stronger opinion on issues, and are more likely to share news if they have a strong opinion on the issue mentioned in the news.

We demonstrate that the family of subgroups consisting of piecewise linear homeomorphisms for Nivat's theorem's proof is equivalent to an infinitesimal version of the Braised Chicken subset within the R. Thompson group V, thereby showing this association to yield a soluble version of a previously stated conjecture regarding V's polynomial growth. Additionally, by relating the homeomorphisms' path complexity to generating pair lengths, we establish an open question related to Nivat's problem.

A quantum system, which is part of a larger environment, responds differently to two types of driving methods: continuous periodic driving and periodic square pulse driving. The first type of driving, unlike the second, does not allow for the observation of a steady condition where the population returns to a specific value due to symmetry. Steady conditions can, however, be identified with periodic square pulse driving. Our theory confirms that it is possible to achieve a driven steady condition through periodic square pulse driving by analyzing a Rabi model with a large number of operations per cycle and demonstrates that this phenomenon is relevant for various types of two-level systems, including quantum dots and superconducting qubits. Our research also offers a framework that could be used to identify a steady condition in a qubit by measuring the entropy of its connection to a larger environmental space.

We explore how several recurring operators including reflection, extension, and superposition affect biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. Specifically, we establish how these operators impact the classification of biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space following the method introduced by Chen and we examine biharmonic hypersurfaces with high symmetry. Furthermore, we determine the conditions under which these hypersurfaces can be classified through the same method in the Euclidean space.

A set of points represented by rational numbers is considered fully distinguishable if a function that maps each point to a corresponding integer is unique. Determining the maximum number of points that can be efficiently identified by using a function that maps each point to a corresponding integer in the form of p/q is the subject of this research. It has already been established that this maximum number is 2d+1 when the denominator is limited to d distinct values. It has been proven that this 2d+1 identification capacity is achievable with points labeled by powers of a specific irrational number and it has been proven that it is also asymptotically reachable as the denominator becomes infinitely large which means the collection of points labeled by 1,a,a^2,...,a^(q-1) can identify 2d+1 values for any fixed irrational number a. It has been found that when the denominator is infinitely large, the capacity approaches infinity at a rate of approximately \sqrt{2k} log(k) where k represents the number of distinct identifiers. It has been proven that the asymptotic rate of growth for identifying collections of powers of different irrational numbers is the same when the denominator is limited to a fixed number. It has been proven that the asymptotic rate of growth for identifying collections of different irrational numbers with the same denominator is the same when the denominator is infinitely large which means the same identity holds for both finite and infinitely large denominations.
